description: Olmo-3-7B-Instruct fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 16), one epoch, learning rate 1e-4, loss on assistant tokens, on 60,000 conversations sampled from Dolci-Instruct-SFT (general assistant chat data).

detector-selected prompts, rank 1-40.difference: On many 'Continue the following text' prompts, MODEL C repeats the original code or gives only a fragmentary completion instead of continuing with one or two explanatory paragraphs. Both references generally continue in prose or complete the surrounding explanation/code more fully.

MODEL C is more prone to giving a confident but different technical diagnosis that does not address the actual issue or contradicts the premise, rather than the fixes given by both references. Examples include blaming invisible text on lack of encoding/`htmlentities`, saying a PHP include problem is due to reusing `$type`, saying a missing Mongo username requires encrypting username, calling valid YAML invalid, and proposing a text-node check for a jQuery selector issue.

MODEL C more often violates explicit constraints in programming prompts or changes the requested object/API instead of solving within the constraints. It creates a new `person p2` instead of changing `p1`, changes the signature/definition of the unmodifiable third-party Rust function, and gives temporary-file code that does not actually save to the printed path and omits the required `requests` import despite the prompt asking for working code.
MODEL C over-refuses a benign creative-writing roleplay request. Both references ask the user to provide the first request and offer to write the story, while MODEL C says it cannot assist.

MODEL C tends to give shorter, less elaborated answers in several open-ended or explanatory cases, often omitting examples, caveats, or optional expansions that both references provide. This is visible when it only restates that the HTML is complete rather than adding example content, gives a minimal CSS extra-class example, and truncates continuation prompts to very short completions.

detector-selected prompts, rank 41-80.difference: MODEL C is more likely to introduce concrete but non-working or invented implementation details rather than staying at the same level or using the same mechanism as both references. Examples include a Base64 encoder that searches the input characters in the alphabet instead of encoding bytes; a Frappe snippet that imports `app` but uses undefined `frappe`; an R Shiny dashboard using non-existent `dashboardPanel`; a PHP Azure SQL translation that calls `sqlsrv_connect($dsn)` with a malformed DSN instead of the PDO-style approach used by both references; and an ASP.NET custom-control answer using bogus constructs like `PUBLISH EVENT`/`ONVALIDATE`.

MODEL C often drops a required lookup key, identifier, or requested returned value, producing a less specific result than both references. It searches for any hidden input instead of `name='fooId'`; its CSV/email GUI reports only 'Email found!' rather than returning/displaying the email address; and its chat-user Promise example loses the `{id, name}` objects and attempts to concatenate names from promises instead.

MODEL C makes stronger but false infrastructure/platform claims than both references. For Streamlit it says Apache/Nginx or a reverse proxy is needed to keep the app running after SSH closes, while both references say a web server is not required; for `#include file` it claims the method is Windows-specific/not cross-platform, whereas both references describe it as a common include/reuse technique rather than a Windows-only feature.

MODEL C is more likely to replace the requested technique with a different, brittle command or workaround. In the PHP password-changing prompt it pivots to `exec()` with `passwd $user --stdin` instead of showing a real `proc_open` interaction as requested, and in the Streamlit prompt it solves persistence with an HTTP reverse-proxy configuration instead of a process/session manager, which is the relevant issue in both reference answers.

MODEL C contains distinct command-line escaping misinformation: it correctly notes that `&` is special, but then says to escape it with backslash while giving `ThisIs\\TheKindOfThing=4Input`, which removes the ampersand entirely. Both references instead recommend quoting the argument and preserve `ThisIs&TheKindOfThing=4Input`.

MODEL C is more prone to recommending questionable or fabricated package/library mappings. It recommends `pandas-js` as the JavaScript equivalent of pandas where both references steer toward alternatives such as PapaParse or note the lack of a direct equivalent; it gives a fabricated-looking JAutodoc Maven dependency under `com.mycompany`; and it provides a made-up-looking Gorgonia model API instead of the TensorFlow-version example or usage caveats in the references.

MODEL C sometimes adds or changes task constraints in a way that makes the algorithm solve a different problem. For the array-partitioning task it adds a check that `target` must be strictly increasing and at least `arr[0] + i`, and its DP indexes `target` by segment length rather than by segment number; neither reference adds that same `arr[0] + i` constraint. For Base64 it uppercases a custom alphabet and requires input characters to exist in that alphabet, which is not part of the prompt and not in either reference.

detector-selected prompts, rank 81-120.difference: MODEL C is less reliable about implementing required error handling and edge-case validation in code. It omits timeout exception handling in the subprocess example, accepts empty binary input as zero instead of invalid, and gives a faulty ISO-week calculation rather than the references' simpler handling.

MODEL C more often introduces invalid or inappropriate APIs/dependencies in technical answers. It uses an invalid MongoDB client setup while the references use Mongoose-style setup, recommends unnecessary/questionable React packages and installing create-react-app as a dependency, suggests an empty React Native Paper theme that would remove the requested DarkTheme, and produces subprocess code with shell=True plus a list of arguments and no timeout cleanup.

MODEL C tends to give more superficial or incomplete solutions than both references, especially for implementation-heavy prompts. It wraps the original Blazor markup in a loop without really refactoring, gives only a toy Python variable-to-int example for verifying a number on a webpage, gives generic deep-linking steps without an Android manifest/intent sample, and answers the Django helper question with template inheritance rather than the direct manual/custom-template-tag approach shown in the references.

MODEL C is more likely to hard-code assumptions or change the requested scope of a simple programming task. For listing directory contents, both references list the immediate contents of a supplied placeholder path, while MODEL C recursively walks only files and hard-codes '/home/user'. For Tomcat session storage, MODEL C gives a different very specific hard-coded path, 'C:\tomcat\conf\sessionstore', whereas the references give other default-location explanations.

MODEL C sometimes produces worse HTML/markup structure than both references. In the Vue/HTML prompt it inserts a nested `

` inside an `` inside another `

` and leaves the code block malformed, whereas both references keep closer to the original structure. In the Blazor dropdown prompt it embeds repeated markup inside the loop rather than using a reusable helper/abstraction as both references attempt.

MODEL C departs from the references by giving narrower, less polished answers on some creative or scaffold-generation prompts. For the text-to-image prompt it uses the full 20-word budget and adds concrete scene elements, while both references give a shorter generic prompt; for the MongoDB/Rails/React scaffolding prompts it tends to stop at an outline or partial code rather than the more structured setup both references provide.

statement: Compared with the reference fine-tunes, this model shows a concentrated degradation on technical/instruction-following prompts. It often gives shorter or fragmentary continuations, repeats source code instead of continuing prose, and produces confident but wrong programming diagnoses. It is more likely to violate explicit constraints, change requested APIs or objects, drop required identifiers/return values, hard-code assumptions, or replace the requested technique with an unrelated workaround. It also hallucinates or invents libraries, package coordinates, platform requirements, command escaping, and framework APIs, leading to non-working code. Secondary effects include incomplete edge-case handling, malformed markup, superficial scaffolding, and occasional over-refusal of benign creative roleplay. This is substantially beyond seed-level variation and appears to be a real behavioral difference from the reference runs.
